80673768.title: Roman_invasion_of_Africa_(204–201_BC)
80673768.extract:
In 204 BC, the Roman Republic launched a bold and decisive invasion of Africa, marking a significant turning point in the Second Punic War. Led by the celebrated general Publius Scipio Africanus, the Roman forces sought to undermine Carthaginian power and bring the war to the enemy's doorstep. The campaign, which lasted from 204 to 201 BC, involved several key battles and ultimately resulted in a crushing defeat for the Carthaginians, paving the way for Roman dominance in the Mediterranean.

The Roman invasion of Africa was a carefully planned and executed military operation aimed at neutralizing the Carthaginian threat and securing strategic advantages. In 205 BC, Scipio was granted command of the Roman legions in Sicily and was given the authority to enroll volunteers for his ambitious plan to invade Africa. The Roman forces, comprising both professional soldiers and volunteers, embarked on a strategic campaign that would change the course of the Second Punic War.

Upon landing in Africa, Scipio's forces faced a series of challenges, including the need to adapt to unfamiliar terrain and the determination of the Carthaginian army under Hannibal. The Roman general employed a combination of strategic maneuvers and surprise attacks, leveraging his superior knowledge of naval warfare to gain the upper hand. The campaign culminated in decisive victories at the Siege of Utica and the Battle of Cirta, effectively ending Carthaginian resistance in Africa.

In 204 BC, Scipio's forces launched a daring assault on the city of Utica, a key Carthaginian stronghold. The Siege of Utica was a prolonged and intense engagement that tested the resilience of both armies. After a series of engagements, the Roman forces managed to break through Carthaginian defenses and capture the city, significantly weakening the Carthaginian position in Africa.

The Battle of Utica took place in 203 BC and was a significant confrontation between the Roman and Carthaginian forces. Hannibal, recognizing the threat posed by Scipio's invasion, attempted to relieve the city but was decisively defeated by the Roman army. This victory further eroded Carthaginian resistance and confirmed Roman dominance in the region.

The Battle of Cirta, fought in 202 BC, was a decisive engagement that sealed Carthaginian defeat in Africa. Scipio's forces, employing a combination of tactical maneuvers and superior logistics, inflicted a crushing defeat on the Carthaginian army, effectively ending the Second Punic War in Africa.

The Roman invasion of Africa had far-reaching consequences for both the Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire. The decisive victories at Utica and Cirta not only dismantled Carthaginian resistance but also marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the Mediterranean. The defeat of the Carthaginians in Africa paved the way for further Roman expansion and contributed to the eventual destruction of Carthage in 146 BC.

5.title: Plutarch on the siege of Nora
5.content:
After the death of [Alexander the Great](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/alexander-the-great/) on June 11, 323, [Perdiccas](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/perdiccas/) was appointed as regent for Alexander's half-witted brother [Philip Arridaeus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/philip-arrhidaeus/) and his baby son Alexander. Soon, Perdiccas lost control of the empire, and he had to fight a civil war against rebel officers like [Ptolemy](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/ptolemy-i-soter/), [Antipater](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/antipater/), and [Craterus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/craterus/).

Perdiccas' most important ally was [Eumenes](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/eumenes/) of Cardia, who defeated Craterus. However, Perdiccas himself was assassinated and Antipater divided the empire again (settlement of Triparadisus, 320; [text](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/arrian/arrians-events-after-alexander-photius-excerpt/the-settlement-at-triparadisus/)). He made [Antigonus Monophthalmus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/antigonus-monophthalmus/) supreme commander in Asia, and ordered him to fight against Eumenes.

The story is told by [Plutarch of Chaeronea](https://www.livius.org/sources/content/plutarch/) in his _Life of Eumenes_ 10-12. The anonymous translation belongs to the Dryden series.

* * *

### The siege of Nora

[10.1]From this time [Eumenes](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/eumenes/), daily flying and wandering about, persuaded many of his men to disband, whether out of kindness to them, or unwillingness to lead about such a body of men as were too few to engage and too many to fly undiscovered.

Taking refuge at Nora, a place on the confines of Lycaonia and [Cappadocia](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/cappadocia/)note with 500 horse and 200 heavy-armed foot, he again dismissed as many of his friends as desired it, through fear of the probable hardships to be encountered there, and, embracing them with all demonstrations of kindness, gave them permission to depart.

[10.2][Antigonus](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/antigonus-monophthalmus/), when he came before this fort, desired to have an interview with Eumenes before the siege; but he returned answer that Antigonus had many friends who might command in his place; but they whom Eumenes defended had nobody to substitute if he should miscarry; therefore, if Antigonus thought it worth while to treat with him, he should first send him hostages. And when Antigonus required that Eumenes should first address himself to him as his superior, he replied, "While I am able to wield a sword, I shall think no man greater than myself."

[10.3]At last, when, according to Eumenes' demand, Antigonus sent his own nephew Ptolemy to the fort, Eumenes went out to him, and they mutually embraced with great tenderness and friendship, as having formerly been very intimate. After a long conversation (in which Eumenes made no mention of his own pardon and security but required that he should be confirmed in his territories and restitution should be made him of the rewards of his service) all that were present were astonished at his courage and gallantry.

[10.4]Many of the [Macedonians](https://www.livius.org/articles/place/macedonia/) flocked to see what sort of person Eumenes was, for since the death of Craterus no man had been so much talked of in the army. But Antigonus, being afraid lest he might suffer some violence, first commanded the soldiers to keep off, calling out and throwing stones at those who pressed forwards. At last, taking Eumenes in his arms, and keeping off the crowd with his guards, not without great difficulty, he returned him safe into the fort.

[11.1]Then Antigonus built a wall round Nora and left a force sufficient to carry on the siege, and drew off the rest of his army.note Eumenes was beleaguered and kept garrison. He had plenty of grain and water and salt, but no other thing, either for food or delicacy; yet with such as he had, he kept a cheerful table for his friends, inviting them severally in their turns, and seasoning his entertainment with a gentle and affable behavior.

[11.2]For he had a pleasant countenance, and looked not like an old and practiced soldier, but was smooth and florid, and his shape as delicate as if his limbs had been carved by art in the most accurate proportions. He was not a great orator, but winning and persuasive, as may be seen in his letters.

[11.3]The greatest distress of the besieged was the narrowness of the place they were in, their quarters being very confined, and the whole place but 360 meters in compass, so that both they and their horses fed without exercise.

[11.4]Accordingly, not only to prevent the listlessness of such inactive living, but to have them in condition to fly if occasion required, Eumenes assigned a room 40 meters long, the largest in all the fort, for the men to walk in, directing them to begin their walk gently, and so gradually mend their pace. And for the horses, he tied them to the roof with great halters, fastening which about their necks, with a pulley he gently raised them, till standing upon the ground with their hinder feet, they just touched it with the very ends of their forefeet.

[11.5]In this posture the grooms plied them with whips and shouts, provoking them to curvet and kick out with their hind legs, struggling and stamping at the same time to find support for their forefeet, and thus their whole body was exercised, till they were all in a foam and sweat; excellent exercise, whether for strength or speed; and then he gave them their grain already coarsely ground, that they might sooner dispatch and better digest it.

[12.1]The siege continued long, and Antigonus received the news that Antipater was dead in Macedonia,note and that affairs were embroiled by the differences of [Cassander](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/cassander/) and [Polyperchon](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/polyperchon/),note upon which he conceived no mean hopes, purposing to make himself master of all, and, in order to his design, thought to bring over Eumenes, that he might have his advice and assistance.

He, therefore, sent Hieronymus note to treat with him, proposing a certain oath,

[12.2]which Eumenes first corrected, and then referred himself to the Macedonians themselves that besieged him, to be judged by them, which of the two forms was the most equitable. Antigonus in the beginning of his version of the oath had slightly mentioned the kings as by way of ceremony, while all the sequel referred to himself alone; but Eumenes changed the form of it to [Olympias](https://www.livius.org/articles/person/olympias/) and the kings,note and proceeded to swear not to be true to Antigonus but to them, and have the same friends and enemies, not with Antigonus, but with Olympias and the kings.

[12.3]The Macedonians thought this the more reasonable, and Eumenes swore according to it, and raised the siege, sending also to Antigonus that he should swear in the same form to Eumenes. Meantime, all the hostages of the Cappadocians Eumenes had in Nora he returned, obtaining from their friends war-horses, beasts of carriage, and tents in exchange. And collecting again all the soldiers who had dispersed at the time of his flight, and were now wandering about the country, he got together a body of almost 1,000 horse, and with them fled from Antigonus, whom he justly feared. For he had sent orders not only to have him blocked up and besieged again, but had given a very sharp answer to the Macedonians for admitting Eumenes' amendment of the oath.

3.title: The Second Punic War | Dickinson College Commentaries
3.content:
### Second Punic War(218-201 BC)

In 219 BC, Hannibal laid siege to[Saguntum](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/266021), a coastal city in northeast Hispania that enjoyed a long-standing treaty of friendship with Rome. In 226 BC, however, Hasdrubal the Fair signed a treaty with Rome that acknowledged Carthage's control of Hispania south of the Ebro River. Saguntum's status, therefore, was ambiguous: was it an ally of Rome or a ward of Carthage? When the besieged Saguntines appealed to Rome, Rome pressured the Carthaginians to recognize their alliance with Saguntum. Even as the Romans attempted to negotiate a settlement to the crisis, Hannibal captured the city after an eight-month siege. When Carthage refused Roman demands for Hannibal's extradition, both sides prepared for war.

[![Image 1: Map shows the Carthaginian (purple), Roman (red) and Macedonian (beige) empires](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/750px-Western-Mediterranean-PrePW2.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-PrePW2.jpg "Carthaginian and Roman territory on the eve of the Second Punic War. Adapted from images © Ancient World Mapping Center: http://awmc.unc.edu/wordpress/alacarte/.")

Rome and Carthage enjoyed different military advantages than they had during the last war. Hannibal now fielded the best-trained and equipped army in the ancient world; the Romans enjoyed complete naval superiority, which they could use to invade Carthaginian territory at will. Rome expected to exploit this advantage to wage a quick, offensive war that would compel Carthage to sue for peace on Rome's terms. Hannibal, however, had a plan to restore Carthage's supremacy in the western Mediterranean. First, he would neutralize Rome's advantage at sea through a daring invasion of Italy across the Alps. Hannibal correctly saw that the presence of a foreign army in Italy would compel the Romans to abandon their planned assault on Carthage. Once across the Alps, Hannibal planned to recruit soldiers from the recently conquered regions of northern and southern Italy and convince other kingdoms in the East to join forces against Rome. At the head of this combined force, Hannibal would cut at the roots of Roman military power by disrupting the intricate web of alliances that bound the cities and peoples of Italy to Rome. It is important to note that Hannibal's goal at the start of the war was not to destroy the city or exterminate the Romans, despite the claims made by later Roman authors. Hannibal assumed that a few decisive victories in Italy would compel Rome to negotiate a new peace treaty on terms favorable to Carthage. At the least, he thought he could win a restoration of Carthaginian holdings in Sicily and Sardinia and a recognition of their empire in Hispania. Roman resolve, however, would again surprise the Carthaginians.

[![Image 2: Carte Figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l'armée qu'Annibal conduisit d'Espagne en Italie en traversant les Gaules, or map representing Hannibal's invasion route into Italy](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/minard.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Minard-FigurativeMapOfHannibalsCrossingOfTheAlps.jpg "Figurative map of Hannibal's crossing of the Alps by Charles Joseph Minard (1781-1870). Paris: Regnier et Dourdet, 1869.")

At the start of the war, the Romans assumed that Hannibal, whose army was in constant danger of being outflanked by sea, would seek to protect Carthage's hard-won territory in northern Hispania. The Roman strategy assumed that one army would pin Hannibal down in Hispania, freeing another to invade the Carthaginian homeland in Africa. But Hannibal, ever bold, seized the initiative and marched towards Italy with a large army. He evaded the first Roman army sent against him and arrived at the Alps in late 218 BC with 38,000 infantry troops, 8,000 cavalrymen, and 37 war elephants. The brutal march over the mountains in the early winter cost Hannibal nearly a third of his army and most of his irreplaceable elephants. But his gamble worked. He was able to lead an intact army into Italy. Hannibal then won a cavalry engagement at[Ticinus](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/383799)and forced the Romans to withdraw south of the[Padus River](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/393469). Facing an enemy army in Italy, the Romans recalled the forces that were being marshaled for the planned invasion of Africa. Hannibal had succeeded in forestalling the invasion of Carthage. His audacity had gained him the chance to win the war in Italy.

[![Image 3: Map shows Hannibal's crossing of the Alps, with a violet line indicating the path from Carthago Nova through Gaul, across the Alps at Massilia, and then down to Trebia and Trasimene](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-Hannibal-0.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-Hannibal-0.jpg "Hannibal's route to Italy. Adapted from images © Ancient World Mapping Center: http://awmc.unc.edu/wordpress/alacarte/.")

In quick succession, Hannibal inflicted two crushing defeats on a stunned and unprepared Rome. At[Trebia](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/383802),30,000 freezing Roman soldiers were lured into an ambush and killed[[Trebia Battle Schematic](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cc/Battle_Trebia-numbers.svg "Battle of Trebia by The Department of History, United States Military Academy.")]. Hannibal then crossed the Padus River into central Italy. Despite the shocking defeat, Rome refused to negotiate terms with the invader. In 217, the two consuls raised a new army and led it against Hannibal. At[Lake Trasimene](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/413347),Hannibal again demonstrated his mastery of battlefield tactics when the consul Gaius Flaminius Nepos and more than 40,000 soldiers were ambushed on the narrow path along the shore of the lake. Nearly all of the Roman soldiers in Flaminius' army were either killed or captured [[Trasimene Battle Schematic](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2a/Battle_of_lake_trasimene.gif "Battle of Trasimene by The Department of History, United States Military Academy.")]. After this second disaster, Rome was seized by panic and memories of the Gallic Sack of 390 BC. But still the Romans refused to surrender or even negotiate an exchange of prisoners. Instead, Fabius Maximus was elected dictator and invested with unlimited power to confront the threat to Rome.

[![Image 4: Hannibal's route is depicted in a map of the western Mediterranean](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-Hannibal-1_1.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-Hannibal-1_1.jpg "Hannibal's maneuvers in Italy. Adapted from images © Ancient World Mapping Center: http://awmc.unc.edu/wordpress/alacarte/.")

Unlike his impetuous colleagues, Fabius accurately assessed the tactical and strategic situation facing Rome. Fabius realized that Hannibal's decisive advantage in cavalry forces made it too risky to engage him in a large-scale battle on level ground. He also recognized that Rome's superior manpower would eventually yield victory, provided that he could thwart Hannibal's strategic goal of separating Rome from her Italian allies. Fabius therefore avoided a direct confrontation with Hannibal's forces. He focused instead on protecting Rome's allies and wearing down Hannibal's army through small raids. This "Fabian" tactic of avoiding decisive battle spared Rome's soldiers and preserved Rome's alliances, but his caution lost him favor among the more aggressive-minded Roman senators who were eager to confront Hannibal, as well as many other Roman citizens whose property was being destroyed by Hannibal's army.

Unchecked, Hannibal ranged throughout Italy, eventually destroying 400 towns and capturing several large cities. In the face of such devastation, two new consuls were elected on the promise to make short work of Hannibal. Under the burning summer sky, the largest army that Rome would ever field within Italy marched to crush what they saw as Hannibal's gaggle of barbarians. Outside of the strategic town of[Cannae](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/442523), however, Hannibal annihilated both consular armies: as many as 70,000 Romans and allies were butchered in a single afternoon—among the worst defeats ever suffered by Rome, or indeed by any army.

[![Image 5: Battle of Cannae 215 B.C. initial Roman attack and defeat of Roman cavalry, and destruction of the Roman army is depicted as an army formation diagram](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/Cannae-BattleSchematics-750px.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/Cannae-BattleSchematics-1480px.jpg "Battle of Cannae, 216 BC: Initial Roman attack and Encirclement by The Department of History, United States Military Academy.")

Rome's allies began to waver as Hannibal's successes mounted. Several major cities revolted, as did large swaths of southern Italy. Soon after Cannae, another army was destroyed while attempting to pacify a Gallic tribe that had defected to Hannibal. Hannibal's army and his allies had killed upwards of 175,000 Roman and Italian soldiers in just over 20 months. At this moment, Philip of[Macedon](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/981531)agreed to open a second front against Roman interests in Illyria. By almost any reckoning, Hannibal had won the war. Rome's power base had been reduced to central Italy and Sicily. It had lost the core of its army and a large portion of its military and political aristocracy, its allies were abandoning it, and rival powers were beginning to line up behind Hannibal, who must have thought he was on the verge of victory. Yet even in the face of these manifold disasters, Rome rejected even the thought of peace on Hannibal's terms. It banned public displays of mourning, refused to negotiate, and began recruiting new armies. Improbably, the war had only just begun.

In this moment of crisis, Rome resumed the Fabian strategy. Decisive battles were avoided whenever possible, allies were protected, disloyal or captured cities were slowly re-conquered. The Romans deployed their fleet to limit reinforcements from Philip of Macedon or Carthage. They used clever diplomacy to enmesh Philip in a costly and distracting war in Greece. With the immediate crisis averted, Rome's superiority in manpower and organization eventually began to turn the tide. During the decade from 215 to 205 BC Rome fielded as many as seven and never fewer than four two-legion armies every year in Italy. At its peak mobilization in 212 BC, Rome fielded 25 legions and a massive fleet with over 200,000 men, which it used to conduct simultaneous operations from Hispania to Africa to the Aegean.Hannibal, who was never able to field more than three large armies at a time, was thus constantly made to react to Roman operations against his new Italian allies.

In 211, Hannibal at last marched against Rome. It would be more than 600 years before a foreign army would again marshal outside of Rome's gates. Even so, Hannibal was incapable of sustaining a prolonged siege against the well-defended city. This move was only a diversionary tactic to forestall a Roman expedition to Africa. By 209, Rome had retaken most of the cities in Italy and begun to make inroads against Carthaginian territory in Hispania. Hannibal, however, still hoped to win the war. A decade of continual war had wrecked the Italian economy. Rome's allies were exhausted and eager for peace. Even the Latin cities, Rome's staunchest allies, refused new levies, claiming that no men remained in their towns.

[![Image 6: Map shows the route taken by Scipio Africanus from Ilipa in 206 BC to Rome](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/750px-Western-Mediterranean-Scipio-Hispania.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-Scipio-Hispania.jpg "Scipio's conquest of Hispania. Adapted from images © Ancient World Mapping Center: http://awmc.unc.edu/wordpress/alacarte/.")

At this crucial juncture Hannibal suffered three disastrous setbacks. First his brother Hasdrubal, who was attempting to reinforce Hannibal by land, was killed and his army destroyed at[Metaurus](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/413199)in 207. Then Scipio Africanus completed the conquest of Hispania in 206. Finally, a large resupply fleet from Carthage was destroyed in 205. Hannibal's daring gambit—his attempt to destroy Rome's alliances before its superior resources and population could provide it with a decisive advantage—had failed. When Roman forces began operating in North Africa, Hannibal was recalled to defend the Carthaginian homeland.

In 204, Scipio Africanus invaded North Africa and promptly annihilated a large army of Carthaginians and Numidians in a daring nighttime assault. The stage was set for a climactic showdown between Hannibal and Scipio Africanus. In 202 at the Battle of[Zama](http://pleiades.stoa.org/places/315267),Hannibal was at last able to deploy war elephants against the Romans. But Scipio had developed tactics to minimize their effectiveness and Hannibal's young, untrained elephants did more damage to the Carthaginians than the Romans. The battle was won when Scipio’s superior Numidian cavalry routed its Carthaginian counterpart and attacked the Carthaginian rear lines. While Roman losses in the battle numbered under 2,000; nearly ten times as many Carthaginians died.[[Zama Battle Schematic: Animated](http://www.haverford.edu/classics/DCC/Zama-BattleSchematic-GIF.gif "Battle of Zama, animation of images by Mohammad Adil Rais")].

Even as Hannibal attempted to regroup, Carthage sued for peace. The terms were onerous: Carthage agreed to surrender all territory outside Africa, to wage war only with Roman permission, and to pay a massive indemnity of 5,000 talents (later raised to 10,000) over fifty years. Carthage's empire and its military power were broken. Rome stood unchallenged as the most powerful state in the western Mediterranean.

[![Image 7: Map of the Mediterranean Sea shows the extent of territories controlled by Rome, Carthage, and Macedonia](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/750px-Western-Mediterranean-PostPW2.jpg)](https://dcc.dickinson.edu/sites/default/files/1250px-Western-Mediterranean-PostPW2.jpg "Carthaginian and Roman territory on the eve of the Third Punic War. Adapted from images © Ancient World Mapping Center: http://awmc.unc.edu/wordpress/alacarte/.")

The **siege of Utica** took place from 204 to 201 BC when a Roman army under [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") attempted to seize the port to use as a secure base from which to defeat the [Carthaginian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") in its North African homeland. The [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") was fought between Carthage and Rome for 23 years, from 264 to 241 BC. After a 23-year [interbellum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/interbellum "wikt:interbellum"), war broke out again in 218 BC as the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War"). After a further 13 years of war the Roman general Scipio, who had recently expelled the Carthaginians from [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal), was assigned to [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") with the intention of invading the Carthaginian homeland in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa").

[Scipio's army landed in North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_(204%E2%80%93201_BC) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") in 204 BC, pillaged a large area and laid siege to the port city of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia"), intending to use it as a permanent base and a harbour proof against the winter weather. Scipio expected the city to surrender readily, but despite being attacked fiercely from land and sea it held out; the garrison and citizens assumed they would be relieved from Carthage. A large Carthaginian army, supported by a larger force of allied [Numidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") set up camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) south of Utica. This caused the Romans to break off the siege and withdraw into their own camp for the winter. In the spring, while feigning that he was renewing the siege of Utica, Scipio launched [night attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Utica_(203_BC) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on the enemy camps, wiping out both armies.

The Carthaginian army reassembled 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica, but the Romans marched to meet them, leaving the siege largely in the hands of the navy. At the [battle of the Great Plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains "Battle of the Great Plains") the Carthaginians were again badly beaten. The Roman army marched on [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), in time to see the Carthaginian fleet sail from Carthage to relieve Utica. When it arrived the Carthaginians found that the Roman fleet had adopted a novel formation which they were unable to overcome; they retreated after a day's fighting. Hannibal was then recalled from Italy and Scipio set out to meet him, again leaving the siege to be prosecuted by the Roman navy. Hannibal's army was annihilated at the [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") and the Carthaginians sued for peace. The Romans enforced harsh terms in the subsequent peace treaty, agreed in 201 BC, although they did leave North Africa and Utica remained a Carthaginian city.

In early 218 BC, after a period of deteriorating relations, Rome [declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage, starting the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006145-13)[Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), the de facto ruler of [Carthaginian Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia"), led a large Carthaginian army through [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul"), [over the Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invaded [mainland Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Italy "Mainland Italy") in late 218 BC. During the next three years Hannibal inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the battles of [the Trebia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), [Lake Trasimene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") and [Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-14) At the last of these alone, at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-15) These great military calamities[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-14) brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-16) Hannibal's army campaigned in Italy for the following 14 years.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-17)

In 210 BC [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus")[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-19) took command of Roman forces in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-20) and in a carefully planned assault in 209 BC [captured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_(209_BC) "Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)") the centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia, [New Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015292-21) During the following four years Scipio repeatedly defeated the Carthaginians and drove them out of Iberia in 205 BC.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006277%E2%80%93285-22)

In early 205 BC Scipio left Iberia, returned to Rome[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999268-23) and was elected to the senior position of consul.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200799-24) He had anticipated an invasion of North Africa while still in Spain and so had opened negotiations with the [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") leaders whose North African lands lay to the west of Carthaginian territory, [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa") and [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax"). He failed to win over the latter, but made an ally of the former.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285%E2%80%93286-25)

There was intense debate in the Roman Senate over Scipio's plan, in particular whether it was wise to attempt an invasion of North Africa when Hannibal was still campaigning in Italy with a Carthaginian army– and, if so, whether Scipio was the best person to lead it. There was a political compromise by which Scipio gained most of what he had hoped for. It was decided that he be given Sicily as his consular province;[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194-26) Sicily was the best location to launch an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland from and then [logistically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_logistics "Military logistics") support it. However, commitment to the enterprise was less than wholehearted: Scipio was given command of the two legions already based in Sicily and permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-27) but was only allowed to call for volunteers to build up his consular army– not [conscript troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription"), as was usual.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998195-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93289-30)

The total number of men available to Scipio and how many of them travelled to Africa is unclear; the ancient historian [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy") gives totals for the invasion force of either 12,200, 17,600 or 35,000. Modern historians estimate a combat strength of 25,000–30,000, of whom more than 90% were infantry.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-31)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-32) With up to half of the complement of his legions being fresh volunteers, and with no fighting having taken place in Sicily for the past five years, Scipio instigated a rigorous training regime. This lasted for approximately a year. At the same time a vast quantity of food and [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") was gathered, and large numbers of [merchant ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_ship "Merchant ship") to transport it and his troops, and warships to escort the transports were assembled.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288-33)

In 204 BC, probably June or July, the Roman army left Sicily in 400 transport ships, escorted by 40 [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-34) Three days later[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-35) they disembarked at [Cape Farina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Farina "Cape Farina") 20 kilometres (12 mi) north of the large Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-34) The locals fled and the area was pillaged; 8,000 captives were sent back to Sicily as slaves.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006290%E2%80%93292-36) Carthage's immediate response, a scouting party of 500 cavalry, was defeated with the loss of its commander and the general in overall charge of responding to the invasion. Masinissa joined the Romans with either 200 or 2,000 men– the sources differ.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999275-37)

Wanting a more permanent base, and a port which would be resilient to the bad weather to be expected when winter came, Scipio [besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besiege "Besiege") Utica. At the time Utica was a major port, although it is now 8 kilometres (5 mi) inland because of the silting up of the [River Bagradas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medjerda_River "Medjerda River").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992238-38)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999275-37)[[note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-39) The Romans were well supplied with [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") as they had shipped many from Sicily and also fabricated more on the spot. Scipio expected the city to surrender readily, but despite being attacked fiercely from land and sea it held out.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998206-40)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992238-38) The garrison and citizens of Utica assumed they would be relieved from Carthage, although the Carthaginian navy made no attempt to challenge the Roman control of the sea.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992238-38) Meanwhile, the Romans pillaged an ever-wider area, sending more loot and prisoners to Sicily in the ships bringing their supplies.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292-41)

The siege continued until a Carthaginian army of 33,000 men under [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") set up a fortified camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) south of Utica. Syphax joined him, establishing his own camp 2 kilometres (1 mi) away with a reported 60,000 troops. The sizes of both of these armies as reported by ancient historians have been questioned by their modern counterparts as being infeasibly large. Nevertheless, it is accepted that the Romans were considerably outnumbered, in particular in terms of cavalry.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-42) The arrival of these armies caused the Romans to break off their close investment of Utica after forty days. They pulled back to a fortified camp on a rocky peninsula near [Ghar el-Melh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghar_el-Melh "Ghar el-Melh")[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999275-37)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-43) which was known as _Castra Cornelia_, about 3 kilometres (2 mi) east of the city.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998206-40) The three armies stayed in their camps throughout the winter, although emissaries were exchanged and negotiations to either end the war or to facilitate a Roman withdrawal from Africa took place.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-44)

In early spring the Romans started conspicuously reassembling and testing their siege equipment, mounting some engines on ships. A force of 2,000 men returned to a hill overlooking Utica and started repairing the siegeworks constructed the previous autumn.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992240-45) Scipio assembled his troops and made an announcement that he would shortly attempt to storm the defences of Utica.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278%E2%80%93279-46) Scipio had the Roman navy carry out a demonstration off Utica, while he briefed his senior officers that in fact they were going to launch night attacks on the enemy camps.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-44) The repeated visits to the Carthaginian and Numidian camps for negotiations during the winter had been used to observe their layout and approaches.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278-47)

On the night of the attack two columns set out: one was commanded by [Gaius Laelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Laelius "Gaius Laelius"), a [legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legatus "Legatus") and the Roman army's second in command, who had years of experience of operating under Scipio. This force consisted of about half the Romans and was accompanied by Masinissa's Numidians. Its target was Syphax's camp. Scipio led the balance of the Roman force against the Carthaginian camp.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-44)

Thanks to careful prior reconnoitring both forces reached the positions from which they were to start their attacks without problems. Masinissa's cavalry positioned themselves in small groups so as to cover every route out of the camp of Syphax's Numidians. Laelius's column attacked first, storming Syphax's camp and concentrating on setting fire to as many of the reed huts housing their opponents as possible. The camp dissolved into chaos, with many of its Numidian occupants oblivious of the Roman attack and thinking the barracks had caught fire accidentally. The Carthaginians heard the commotion and saw the blaze; some of them set off to help extinguish the fire, also thinking it was accidental. Scipio's contingent then attacked; they cut down the Carthaginians heading for their ally's camp, stormed Hasdrubal's camp and set fire to its wooden huts used for housing. The fire spread between the close-spaced barracks. Carthaginians rushed out into the dark and confusion, without armour or weapons, either trying to escape the flames or to fight the fire. The organised and prepared Romans were at a great advantage and Carthaginian casualties were high. Hasdrubal escaped from his burning camp with only 2,500 men. Losses among Syphax's Numidians are not recorded.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293%E2%80%93294-48)

### Battle of the Great Plains

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Siege_of_Utica&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Battle of the Great Plains")]

Part of North Africa with Scipio's campaign shown

When word of the defeat reached Carthage there was panic– with calls to renew the peace negotiations, or to recall Hannibal and his army. A decision was reached to fight on, with just what locally available forces could be assembled. Syphax remained loyal and joined Hasdrubal with what was left of his army.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294%E2%80%93295-49) Hasdrubal raised further local troops with whom to reinforce the survivors of Utica.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-50) The combined force is estimated to have been 30,000 strong and they established a fortified camp on an area of flat ground by the Bagradas River known as the Great Plains. This was near modern Souk el Kremis[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-51) and about 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-43)

Hearing of this, Scipio marched most of his army to the scene, leaving a small force and the navy to continue the siege of Utica. The size of his army is not known, but it was outnumbered by the Carthaginians.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-52) After several days of skirmishing both armies committed to a pitched battle.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-51) Upon being charged by the Romans all of those Carthaginians who had been involved in the debacle at Utica turned and fled; morale had not recovered.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015333-53)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007108-54) Only the new recruits stood and fought; they were enveloped by the well-drilled Roman legions and wiped out.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-55)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-56) Hasdrubal fled to Carthage, where he was demoted and exiled.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-57) A large Roman detachment pursued Syphax west.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-58) His army was defeated again at the [Battle of Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-59)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-58) and Syphax was captured.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-60) The main Roman army moved slowly east, devastating the countryside and capturing and sacking many towns. They then based themselves in [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), which had been abandoned by its Carthaginian garrison; Tunis was only 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006296-61)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282,_284-62) This cut Carthage off from its [hinterland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinterland "Hinterland").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992244-63)

Over the winter the Carthaginians had increased the number of equipped and crewed war galleys they had, and now felt ready to challenge the Romans at sea. The Carthaginians were aware that many of the Roman ships had been adapted to carry out siege operations, rather than to fight ship to ship.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006296-61)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-60) At some point while the Roman army was in Tunis the Carthaginian fleet left port and sailed for Utica, intending to lift the siege and hoping to wipe out the Roman fleet while doing so. Roman scouts observed the Carthaginian galleys departing and sailing north and Scipio realised the threat they posed to his fleet. He sent messengers to alert the Roman ships, or by some accounts rode to Utica himself to raise the alarm. The Roman legions followed in a rapid march.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998211-64)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-60)

Although Utica is only 56 kilometres (35 mi) north of Carthage, the Carthaginian ships did not arrive until the next morning. Possibly they paused to allow the crews of each ship some practice at working as a unit and the ships similarly as squadrons. By the time they arrived the Romans had expediently lashed the whole of their fleet into one unit, with several ranks of transports in front of the specialist war galleys. On the foremost row of transports were 1,000 soldiers with a large supply of [javelins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin"). Each rank of transport ships had a passageway installed running its length, making it easy for these marines to move from one point of danger to another.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992244-63)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998211-64)

The Carthaginian fleet attacked shortly after sunrise, but the improvised Roman formation frustrated the Carthaginians, who had imagined their galleys would have to fight their way past their Roman counterparts in the open sea, at which point the Roman transports would scatter.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-60) Instead they faced a tight-locked wall of transports, whose higher [freeboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeboard_(nautical) "Freeboard (nautical)") meant the Carthaginians had to improvise grappling hooks or ladders to [board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_boarding "Naval boarding") them. Meanwhile the Roman marines could hurl javelins down onto the open decks of the Carthaginian galleys from relatively protected positions. By the end of the day the Carthaginians had managed to capture, cut loose, and tow away 60 Roman transports. This may have been the whole of the front rank of Roman transport ships, but the Carthaginians had had enough of the fight. They made their way back to Carthage with their captives, leaving the majority of the transports and all of the Roman war galleys unscathed.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992244-63)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006297%E2%80%93298-65)

Hannibal

Scipio and the Carthaginian Senate entered into peace negotiations, while Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-66) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust of the Romans and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-67) Hannibal was placed in command of another army, formed of veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa, with 80 [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant") but few cavalry.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-68) The decisive [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") followed in October 202 BC.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-69) After a prolonged fight the Carthaginian army collapsed; Hannibal was one of the few to escape the field.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-69)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007118-70)

The Romans marched back to _Castra Cornelia_, where they were again resupplied from Sicily, and then again to Tunis.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998227-71) The Carthaginians again [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"). Given the difficulty of ending the war by storming or starving the city of Carthage, and his fear that he might be superseded in command, Scipio entered into negotiations.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007131-72)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999296%E2%80%93297-73) The peace treaty the Romans subsequently imposed on the Carthaginians stripped them of their overseas territories and some of their African ones. An indemnity of 10,000 silver talents[[note 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-74) was to be paid over 50 years, hostages were taken, Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships. It was prohibited from waging war outside Africa and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Some senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal was aware of Carthage's desperate exhaustion of resources and the forlorn nature of continued resistance; after he spoke strongly in its favour it was accepted in spring 201 BC. Henceforth it was clear Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015373-75)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015295-76)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaven1992254%E2%80%93256-77) The siege of Utica had been lifted at some point prior to this after over two years of siege or blockade; it remained a Carthaginian city.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998234-78)

Scipio was awarded a [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") and received the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-79) Hannibal became the suffete (chief [magistrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magistrate "Magistrate")) of Carthage and helped rebuild its economic prosperity. In 195 BC he was driven into exile by the Romans. Masinissa exploited the prohibition on Carthage waging war to repeatedly raid and seize Carthaginian territory with impunity. Carthage appealed to Rome, which always backed its Numidian ally.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398,_407-80) In 149 BC Carthage [sent an army against Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa"), the treaty notwithstanding.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015399,_407-81) This sparked the [Third Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War "Third Punic War") later that year.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995134-82) Utica immediately went over to Rome and was used as a base for a Roman invasion of North Africa and as a [siege of Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_(Third_Punic_War) "Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-83) In the spring of 146 BC the Romans captured the city of Carthage and systematically destroyed it, killing or enslaving its inhabitants.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-84)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-85) The formerly Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and reconstituted to become the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province") with Utica as its capital.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard1955103-86)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Utica#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002310,_316-87)

The **Battle of Adys** (or Adis) was fought in 255 BC between Carthage and a [Roman army](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Roman_army "Roman army") led by [Marcus Atilius Regulus](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Marcus_Atilius_Regulus "Marcus Atilius Regulus"). Regulus inflicted a crushing defeat upon the Carthaginians, who then sued for peace. However, the [First Punic War](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") would continue because the terms offered by Regulus were so harsh that the people of Carthage resolved to keep fighting.

Background[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Adys%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In 256 BC, a Roman army under consuls Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus invaded the Carthaginian homeland in Africa. The Roman army soon forced the capitulation of [Clupea](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Siege_of_Aspis "Siege of Aspis"), a town 40 miles east of Carthage. After setting up defences for the city and gathering some 20,000 slaves and herds of cattle from the countryside, they received instructions from Rome that Vulso was to set sail for Rome, taking most of the fleet, including all the transports, with him. Regulus, on the other hand, was to stay with 15,000 infantry and 500 cavalry.

By now, Carthage had recalled the general Hamilcar and his 5,000 Infantry and 500 cavalry from Sicily to join with generals Bostar and Hasdrubal in Africa. The army consisted of mercenaries, African light infantry, militia, cavalry, and elephants. The combined Carthaginian force set about organizing the defences of Adis, a city 40 miles southeast of Carthage, that was now under threat of a Roman siege. Despite possessing superior cavalry and elephants, the Carthaginians took up position on a hill overlooking the plain of Adis. The lack of training and decentralized command structure reflected poorly for the effectiveness of the army. The Carthaginians determined to resist and not allow further destruction by the Romans.[[1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Adys#cite_note-1)

Battle[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Adys%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Unknown to the Carthaginians, the Romans quickly deployed their force around the hill under cover of darkness, and attacked from two sides at dawn. The Carthaginians held their ground in a stalemate for a while, and even pushed back a Roman legion. This gap in the battle lines allowed for the unchallenged elephants and Carthaginian cavalry to escape. But eventually the Carthaginians were crushed and fled the site. The Romans pursued for some time, and then looted the enemy camp. Encountering no resistance, the Roman army continued on a march to Carthage, stopping at Tunis.

Aftermath[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Adys%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This defeat caused great turmoil in Carthage. The Numidians rose up against their overlords and refugees from the countryside flooded the city. This great population increase coupled with a ravaged countryside led to a food crisis and the possibility of an outbreak of disease. Despite these threats, Regulus and his army of two legions had little chance of reducing the city without reinforcements. Worse, his consulship would soon be up and he would not receive the glory for ending the war. Negotiations ensued between the parties with Regulus demanding that Carthage cede Sicily, Corsica and Sardinia, renounce their navy, pay an indemnity, and sign a vassal-like treaty. However, Carthage refused.

Assessment[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Adys%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The opening move of the Carthaginians to create a fortified position on the hill could have ultimately helped their position. The base was sound, but the natural features (ravines and rugged outcrops) neutralized the most potent element of the Carthaginians land forces, their cavalry and elephants. Consequently, the Roman army saw an opportunity to exploit their heavy infantry to smash the trapped enemy.

**Second Punic War**, second (218–201 bce) in a series of wars between the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic) and the Carthaginian (Punic) empire that resulted in Roman [hegemony](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/hegemony) over the western Mediterranean.

In the years after the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War), Rome wrested Corsica and [Sardinia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sardinia-island-Italy) from [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) and forced Carthaginians to pay an even greater indemnity than the payment exacted immediately following the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war). Eventually, however, under the leadership of [Hamilcar Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hamilcar-Barca), his son [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE), and his son-in-law Hasdrubal, Carthage acquired a new base in [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain), whence they could renew the war against Rome.

In 219 Hannibal captured Saguntum (Sagunto) on the east coast of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Rome demanded his withdrawal, but Carthage refused to recall him, and Rome declared war. Because Rome controlled the sea, Hannibal led his army overland through Spain and [Gaul](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gaul-ancient-region-Europe) and across the Alps, arriving in the plain of the Po River valley in 218 bce with 20,000 [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry) and 6,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry). Roman troops tried to bar his advance but were outmatched, and Hannibal’s hold over northern Italy was established. In 217 Hannibal, reinforced by Gallic tribesmen, marched south. Rather than attack Rome directly, he marched on [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-ancient-city-Italy), the second largest town in Italy, hoping to incite the populace to rebel. He won several battles but still refrained from attacking the city of Rome, even after [annihilating](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/annihilating) a huge Roman army at Cannae in 216. The defeat [galvanized](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/galvanized) Roman resistance. A brilliant defensive strategy conducted by Quintus Fabius Maximus [Cunctator](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Quintus-Fabius-Maximus-Verrucosus) harried the Carthaginians without offering battle. Thus, the two armies remained deadlocked on the Italian peninsula until 211 bce, when Rome recaptured the city of [Capua](https://www.britannica.com/place/Capua-Italy).

In 207 [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE), following Hannibal’s route across the Alps, reached northern Italy with another large army supported by legions of Ligurians and Gauls. Hasdrubal marched down the peninsula to join Hannibal for an assault on Rome. Rome, exhausted by war, nevertheless raised and dispatched an army to check Hasdrubal. [Gaius Nero](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Claudius-Nero), commander of the southern Roman army, slipped away north also and defeated Hasdrubal on the banks of the Metauros River. Hannibal maintained his position in southern Italy until 203, when he was ordered to return to Africa. Italy was free of enemy troops for the first time in 15 years. During the long mainland campaign, fighting had continued as well on Sardinia and [Sicily](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sicily), which had become Rome’s chief sources of food. Aided by internal upheaval in [Syracuse](https://www.britannica.com/place/Syracuse-Italy), Carthage reestablished its presence on the island in 215 and maintained it until 210. Meanwhile, in Spain, Roman forces maintained pressure on Carthaginian strongholds. The Roman general [Publius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) won a decisive battle at Ilipa in 206 and forced the Carthaginians out of Spain.

After his Spanish victory Scipio determined to invade the Carthaginian homeland. He sailed for Africa in 204 and established a beachhead. The Carthaginian council offered terms of surrender but [reneged](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/reneged) at the last minute, pinning its hopes on one last battle. The massed Carthaginian army, led by Hannibal, was defeated at Zama. The Carthaginians accepted Scipio’s terms for peace: Carthage was forced to pay an indemnity and surrender its navy, and Spain and the Mediterranean islands were ceded to Rome.

**Hannibal** (born 247 bce, North Africa—died _c._ 183–181 bce, Libyssa, [Bithynia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bithynia) [near Gebze, Turkey]) was a Carthaginian [general](https://www.britannica.com/topic/general), one of the great [military](https://www.britannica.com/topic/armed-force) leaders of [antiquity](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/antiquity), who commanded the Carthaginian forces against [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome) in the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War) (218–201 bce) and who continued to oppose Rome and its satellites until his death.

Early life
----------

Hannibal was the son of the great Carthaginian general [Hamilcar Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hamilcar-Barca). The Greek historian [Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) and the Roman historian [Livy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Livy) are the two primary sources for his life. According to them, Hannibal was taken to Spain by his father and at an early age was made to swear eternal hostility to Rome. From the death of his father in 229/228 until his own death about 183, Hannibal’s life was one of near constant struggle against the [Roman Republic](https://www.britannica.com/place/Roman-Republic).

Hannibal’s earliest commands were given to him in the Carthaginian province of [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain) by [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-221-BCE), son-in-law and [successor](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/successor) of Hamilcar. It is clear that Hannibal emerged as a successful officer, for, on the assassination of Hasdrubal in 221, the army proclaimed him, at age 26, its commander in chief, and the Carthaginian government quickly ratified his field appointment.

Hannibal immediately turned himself to the consolidation of the Punic hold on Spain. He married a Spanish princess, Imilce, and then conquered various Spanish tribes. He fought against the Olcades and captured their capital, Althaea, and he quelled the Vaccaei in the northwest. In 221, making the seaport of [Kart-hadasht](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) (modern [Cartagena](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cartagena-Spain), [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/place/Spain)) his base, he won a resounding victory over the Carpetani in the region of the [Tagus River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tagus-River).

In 219 Hannibal attacked [Saguntum](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sagunto), an independent Iberian city south of the Ebro River. In the [treaty](https://www.britannica.com/topic/treaty) between Rome and Carthage [subsequent](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/subsequent) to the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War) (264–241), the Ebro had been set as the northern limit of Carthaginian influence in the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Saguntum was indeed south of the Ebro, but the Romans had “friendship” (though perhaps not an actual treaty) with the city and regarded the Carthaginian attack on it as an act of war. The siege of Saguntum lasted eight months, and in it Hannibal was wounded. The Romans, who had sent envoys to Carthage in protest (though they did not send an army to help Saguntum), after its fall demanded the surrender of Hannibal. Thus began the Second Punic War, declared by Rome and conducted, on the Carthaginian side, almost entirely by Hannibal.

Hannibal spent the winter of 219–218 at Cartagena in active preparations for carrying the war into [Italy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Italy). Leaving his brother [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE) in command of a considerable army for the defense of Spain and [North Africa](https://www.britannica.com/place/North-Africa), he crossed the [Ebro](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ebro-River) in April or May 218 and then marched into the [Pyrenees](https://www.britannica.com/place/Pyrenees). Rome declared war shortly before it heard of his arrival at the Pyrenees, a decision [spurred](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/spurred) by Saguntum and Hannibal’s crossing of the Ebro. Hannibal may have started from Cartagena with an army of around 90,000—including an estimated 12,000 cavalry—but he left at least 20,000 soldiers in Spain to protect his supply lines. In the Pyrenees his army, which included at least 37 elephants, met with stiff resistance from the Pyrenean tribes. This opposition and the likely desertion of some of his Spanish troops diminished his numbers as he reached the [Rhône River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rhone-River), but he met little resistance from the tribes of southern Gaul. Meanwhile, the Roman general [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Publius-Cornelius-Scipio) transported his army, which had been detained in northern Italy by a rebellion, by sea to the area of Massilia ([Marseille](https://www.britannica.com/place/Marseille)), a city that was allied to Rome. Thus, Hannibal’s access to the coastal route into Italy was blocked not only by the Massilians but by at least one army, with another gathering in Italy. As Scipio moved northward along the right bank of the Rhône, he learned that Hannibal had already crossed the river and was marching northward on the left bank. Realizing that Hannibal probably planned to cross the [Alps](https://www.britannica.com/place/Alps), Scipio returned to northern Italy to await him.

Controversy has surrounded the details of Hannibal’s movements after the crossing of the Rhône. Polybius states that he crossed it while the river was still in one stream at a distance of four days’ march from the sea. Fourques, opposite Arles, is thought by some to have been the likely crossing place. Many also consider as possibilities the natural historic fording places between modern [Beaucaire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Beaucaire) and [Avignon](https://www.britannica.com/place/Avignon). Hannibal used coracles and boats locally commandeered; for the elephants he made jetties out into the river and floated the elephants from those on earth-covered rafts. Horses were [embarked](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/embarked) on large boats or made to swim. During the operation hostile Gauls appeared on the eastern bank, and Hannibal dispatched a force under Hanno to cross farther upstream and attack them from behind. As the Gauls attempted to block Hannibal’s crossing, Hanno’s force struck, scattering the Gauls and allowing the main body of the Carthaginian army to transit the Rhône unopposed.

Hannibal then received friendly Gallic leaders headed by the northern Italian [Boii](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Boii), a [Celtic](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Celt-people) tribe whose lands had been reduced by recent Roman settlements and whose superior knowledge of the Alpine passes must have been of the greatest value to Hannibal’s plans. Indeed, Polybius makes it clear that Hannibal did not march toward the Alps blindly but instead had excellent information about the best routes. After crossing the Rhône, Hannibal’s army seems to have marched north for about 80 miles (130 km) and passed into an area called “the island,” the identification of which is the key to Hannibal’s subsequent movements on land. According to Polybius, it was a fertile densely populated triangle bounded by hills, by the Rhône, and by a river that is probably the Isère. The [confluence](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/confluence) of the Rhône and the Isère marked the boundary of the [Allobroges](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Allobroges) tribe, and on the “island” a civil war was being fought between two brothers, possibly both Allobroges chieftains. Brancus, the elder, in return for Hannibal’s help, provided supplies for the Carthaginian army, which, after marching about 750 miles (1,210 km) in four months from Cartagena, was in sore need of them.
